item.title: Brands turn to AI micro dramas to engage consumers in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
BEIJING, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- A young woman browses the drinks aisle of a convenience store, picks up a beverage and finds herself drawn into a budding romance. The scene unfolds in a micro drama released by convenience store chain FamilyMart in China, as the company explores ways to engage consumers through artificial intelligence (AI)-generated entertainment. Such productions illustrate an emerging trend in China's brand marketing, with companies using AI-generated characters and settings to weave products and brand messages into storylines, making commercial content part of the viewing experience. China's micro drama market exceeded 100 billion yuan (about 14.9 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, and the country had more than 800 million micro-drama users as of September this year, according to the National Radio and Television Administration. In the first eight months of 2026, some 430,000 micro dramas were released, 13 times the total for all of 2025, with AI-generated productions accounting for more than 90 percent, the administration said. Major platforms are exploring the format's commercial potential. Hongguo Short Drama launched an AI micro-drama creation program in October that includes matchmaking between creators and brands for commercial projects, while Taobao has partnered with consumer brands to produce AI-generated promotional series. MICRO DRAMAS, LONG-TERM CONSUMER TIES Micro dramas typically rely on plot twists and dramatic conflicts to capture viewers' attention within minutes, but consumer brands are using the format with longer-term marketing goals in mind. After releasing two seasons of live-action micro dramas, FamilyMart is now using AI to produce a series titled "Healing Moments at the Convenience Store," with the technology enabling the company to explore more settings and camera techniques at lower production costs. In line with its strategy of catering to five eating occasions throughout the day, FamilyMart has developed stories around five aspects of everyday life, namely work, communities, personal growth, romance and school. The dramas feature products such as coffee, sandwiches, oden (a Japanese-style simmered dish) and steamed buns for immediate consumption. Unlike short videos and livestream shopping, which excel at generating product interest and immediate sales, respectively, AI-generated micro dramas offer complete narratives in which stores, employees, food and services can naturally become part of the characters' everyday lives, said Li Hao, the company's public relations director. Through AI micro dramas, FamilyMart seeks to translate online interest into store visits, coupon redemptions and repeat purchases through its membership program. "Products must appear at moments when they are needed," Li said, adding that membership benefits and payment discounts should help advance the plot. The company plans to evaluate the effectiveness of its dramas by tracking viewing behavior, brand recognition and business indicators such as product searches and new memberships, with comparisons across different regions and time periods. Cosmetics brand Pechoin, founded in Shanghai in 1931, began exploring micro dramas after noticing that traditional in-feed advertisements on platforms such as Douyin had reached a plateau in effectiveness, while micro dramas were performing better in terms of exposure, click-through rates and user interaction. Wang Lujun, the company's head of content marketing, said micro dramas can reach a much larger audience than conventional in-feed advertisements on the same budget, with interested viewers then directed to livestreaming sessions for product purchases. Pechoin produces two types of AI micro dramas. One draws on popular themes such as rebirth and second chances in workplace and everyday settings to attract potential customers, while the other focuses on product promotions during major shopping festivals such as Singles' Day, targeting consumers already familiar with the brand and inclined to make repeat purchases. With consumers increasingly familiar with skincare ingredients and their functions, simply presenting ingredient data is becoming less effective in a highly competitive market crowded with similar products, Wang said. Targeting mainly consumers aged 25 to 45, Pechoin uses fictional stories to explain how products work and present test data in the context of everyday skincare concerns, such as the effects of staying up late and early signs of aging. CONTENT AS A STOREFRONT Consumers are growing wary of direct sales pitches but remain receptive to discovering products through content they choose to watch, said Tang Jiansheng, a Shanghai-based senior expert in consumer insights and business analysis. In traditional e-commerce, consumers typically search for products they need and compare prices before buying. Livestream shopping, meanwhile, often generates purchases through hosts' recommendations and promotional offers. Micro dramas offer a different route to consumption, with viewers potentially developing an interest in a product through the storyline, Tang said. Consumers' sense of connection with a product is becoming an increasingly important factor in purchasing decisions, alongside price and functionality, Tang added. In an AI-generated animated series jointly launched by Taobao, Tmall and Blue Moon, a manufacturer of household and personal care products, a young office worker sets off on a holiday with a magical creature summoned from a pump bottle of body wash, turning a product feature into a plot device. Recommendation algorithms allow brands to reach consumers more cost-effectively based on their interests and recent searches, while shopping functions embedded in entertainment platforms can shorten the path from product discovery to purchase, Tang said. Tang cited a feature linking Hongguo Short Drama to Douyin's e-commerce services, which allows viewers to pause a drama, search for products similar to those on screen and place orders. Tang described the emerging model as a scalable content-based storefront and said that AI also allows brands to quickly test how different storylines, product selling points and consumption scenarios affect purchasing decisions among different consumer groups, increasing investment in versions that generate better sales results. In the future, the same brand could produce different versions of a micro drama for mothers with young children, office workers and older consumers, with tailored plots and product placements. Brands could also use AI to analyze viewer comments and interactions to improve their products, Tang added. LOWER COSTS, HIGHER CONTENT STANDARDS The rapid expansion of AI-generated micro dramas has exposed a gap between production volume and audience interest. During this year's Spring Festival period, live-action micro dramas generated 25 times the total views of AI-generated micro dramas, despite having only about one-fiftieth as many new releases, according to an article published on the website of the China Netcasting Services Association. For brands seeking to capture viewers' attention, lower production costs make it easier to experiment with different types of content. Wang said Pechoin can produce dozens of episodes in batches to test audience responses, introduce more characters and create settings such as polar regions that would be costly or difficult to film. Savings on production could also be redirected toward promotional offers and gifts for consumers, Wang added. However, industry insiders stressed that as production becomes easier, creativity, an understanding of consumer needs and product authenticity become increasingly important. "The cheaper content becomes, the scarcer attention becomes. Ultimately, competition comes down to creativity and genuine consumer insights," Tang said. Pechoin, for example, draws on customer service feedback and product reviews to identify skincare concerns before developing scripts. It also devotes particular attention to refining AI-generated skin textures to avoid unrealistic depictions of product effects, Wang said. FamilyMart, meanwhile, aims to reduce spending on sets, actor fees and special effects, while maintaining investment in character development, storytelling and accurate product presentation, Li said. In developing FamilyMart's AI series, the creative team interviewed more than 20 convenience store managers, drawing on real-life stories before submitting multiple plot outlines for the brand to review, said Shen Chang, executive producer and director of the series. Although AI has lowered barriers to production, creating micro dramas for brands demands a broad range of skills, from scriptwriting and cinematography to editing and sound design, as creators must balance storytelling, audience emotions and commercial objectives, Shen said. Maintaining consumer trust presents another challenge, with Tang warning that excessive commercialization and blurred boundaries between advertising and entertainment could undermine the credibility of content. FamilyMart requires specialized AI training on product materials and frame-by-frame reviews of footage to ensure that products appear naturally and the brand is accurately represented. The company is also exploring procedures for advertising disclosure, copyright protection and the use of people's likenesses, Li said. "Traffic is a short-lived dividend, while content is an asset that can compound in value for brands," Shen said. ■

item.title: China says U.S. has no say on selection of BBNJ Secretariat seat
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
BEIJING, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese spokesperson said on Wednesday that the United States, which is neither a state party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea nor to the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement, has no say on the selection of the BBNJ Secretariat seat. Guo Jiakun, the spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, made the remarks when asked to comment on a statement issued by the U.S. State Department welcoming the joint bid by Chile and Belgium to host the Secretariat of the BBNJ Agreement. "We call on all parties to stay vigilant against attempts to politicize the bidding and create confrontation in the process," said Guo. He stressed that China has made clear its position on the Belgium-Chile proposal, adding that this joint candidature is problematic in at least six aspects, namely, it contravenes the stipulations of the BBNJ Agreement, procedural justice, established international practice, equitable geographical distribution, fair competition and the original commitment. "According to the BBNJ Agreement, the seat of the Secretariat, the specific modalities for the operation of the Clearing-House Mechanism (CHM), including its installation, as well as where the subsidiary bodies hold their meetings shall all be determined by the Conference of the Parties, and the CHM shall be managed by the Secretariat," said Guo. These are the consensus as well as rights and responsibilities of all Parties to the Agreement, which no country has the right or is in any position to violate, he added. "No one shall trade under the table what should be collectively determined by all Parties, let alone coerce or hijack other Parties into accepting their proposal," Guo noted. As one of the first signatories and Parties to the Agreement and the largest assessed-contributor to its budget, China stands ready to work with the international community to uphold the original purpose of the Agreement and keep the selection of the Secretariat seat proceeding in the right direction, so that the BBNJ Agreement can truly serve the shared interests of humanity, said Guo. ■

item.title: China urges Japan to accelerate destruction of abandoned chemical weapons
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
This photo taken on Nov. 25, 2026 shows the scene of a side event hosted by the Chinese delegation at the 31st Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CSP-31) in The Hague, the Netherlands. China urged Japan to accelerate the destruction of abandoned chemical weapons in China at the CSP-31 in The Hague on Wednesday, stressing that prolonged delays in addressing the issue remain a major practical obstacle to achieving "a world free of chemical weapons." (Xinhua/Shao Haijun) THE HAGUE, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- China urged Japan to accelerate the destruction of abandoned chemical weapons in China at the 31st Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CSP-31) in The Hague on Wednesday, stressing that prolonged delays in addressing the issue remain a major practical obstacle to achieving "a world free of chemical weapons." The Chinese delegation hosted a side event titled "Current Status and Challenges with Respect to the Destruction of the Chemical Weapons Abandoned by Japan on the Territory of China," highlighting delays in the destruction process and calling on Japan to fulfill its obligations under the Convention. More than 100 representatives from over 40 countries attended the event. According to the Chinese delegation, Japan has missed its deadlines for destroying the abandoned chemical weapons four times. The latest plan, adopted in 2022, is due to expire in 2027, putting Japan at risk of missing the deadline for a fifth time. Japan's budget for addressing the abandoned chemical weapons in China was cut by 22 percent this year compared with 2025, even as its defense budget continued to rise. Shen Bo of China's Permanent Representation to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) said discussions at the Conference of the States Parties had reflected several shared understandings within the international community regarding the Japanese abandoned chemical weapons. "Concerns are growing over delays in the destruction process, particularly the risk that Japan could miss the 2027 deadline. The international community expects Japan, as the state that abandoned the weapons, to fulfill its obligations under the Convention and accelerate their destruction," Shen said. He said Japan must adopt a serious and responsible attitude toward its historical, political and legal responsibilities. Any attempt to whitewash its wartime crimes or rewrite history would not be accepted by China or the international community. "Japan must show genuine commitment by faithfully fulfilling its obligations under the Convention and substantially increasing investment in personnel, technology and funding. It must also take swift action by providing accurate information on burial sites, improving the efficiency of excavation and recovery operations, and assuming responsibility for treating contaminated soil and water," Shen told Xinhua after the side event. Vladimir Tarabrin of the Permanent Representation of the Russian Federation to the OPCW said Russia's position on the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan during World War II was "clear and unequivocal." "This is not a matter of Japan's goodwill, nor is it an act of charity. It is Japan's legal and moral obligation to rid itself of this legacy of the Second World War as soon as possible," he added. OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior stressed that recovering and destroying the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan in China is an important part of the international community's shared goal of permanently and completely eliminating chemical weapons worldwide. "This is a difficult task, but one that must be accomplished," she said. ■

item.title: Letter from Lhasa: Keeping cold at bay after southwest China quake
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
by Xinhua writers Lodro Gyatso, Ji Yu and Purbu Tsering LHASA, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- Our glasses fogged up as soon as we stepped into Sonam Dondrup's temporary home. Outside, the wind was bitterly cold, but inside a new stove was burning brightly, with a kettle bubbling away on top of it. Sonam Dondrup, a 54-year-old herder, poured us cups of steaming butter tea and added a small piece of butter, as is customary here. He had grown used to welcoming guests into his new home, a prefabricated shelter on the northern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. A month earlier, on Oct. 22, a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. At an average elevation of more than 4,500 meters, the area was facing a long, bitter winter. After moving into the shelter, Sonam Dondrup's family received a new stove and cooking utensils, and stocked up on heating fuel. "Now we can have hot tea whenever we want," he told us. "I feel at ease knowing we can spend the winter here." Over the course of our visit, we learned how much work had gone to make these shelters habitable for the winter. Namkha Wangpo, head of Nagong Village, told us that village workers had gone door to door checking for gaps in the prefabricated units and sealing them against the cold. They had also settled disputes over living space and tried to find bunk beds for families who needed them. On the doors of the shelters are contact cards in both Tibetan and Chinese, while each household has designated officials to turn to whenever supplies or repairs are needed. By Nov. 22, all residents who needed to be relocated in Maru and Gangchen, the two hardest-hit townships, had moved into temporary shelters. We saw piles of dried yak dung and coal neatly stacked outside the shelters during our trip. Indoors, people took off their heavy winter coats. Nearly 5,500 stoves and more than 1,000 tonnes of heating fuel had been distributed across the earthquake-hit areas, along with some 50,000 bags of rice and flour and over 130 tonnes of fresh vegetables. Around noon in Zaqinda Village of Maru Township, the smell of meat frying with green peppers drew our attention to Gyalpo Dondrup's kitchen. Beside his chopping board he had fresh fruit, vegetables and milk, all supplied by the government. "We even got fresh mutton recently," he told us. "It tasted perfect." Despite the earthquake and the move into temporary housing, people kept up many of their old habits, making yogurt and frying Kasai, a traditional Tibetan pastry made of flour and butter. One young father was particularly happy that he could get infant formula for his baby. The herders also had their animals to worry about as winter approached. A 90-minute drive took us to a pasture in northern Gangchen Township, almost 5,000 meters above sea level. There we met Tsering Loden, 46, who has grazed his animals on this land for 30 years. "Our livestock weren't affected by the earthquake, and we've already stored enough fodder," he said. "We'll be fine this winter." When snow covers the pastures, herders have to rely on the fodder they have stored. The local government has offered subsidies to help herders buy fodder and reached supply agreements with suppliers in neighboring Qinghai Province in northwest China. At a fodder storage facility in Nagong Village, Namkha Wangpo showed us more than 100 tonnes of feed. If severe weather struck, he said, there would be enough emergency feed for every animal in the village. Baqen County head Phuntsog Dondrup described the preparations for winter as securing the "three bags" -- one for heating fuel, one for food and one for fodder. The aim, he said, was to help families get through the winter and rebuild their lives and livelihoods. Nov. 22 was also Minor Snow, one of the 24 solar terms in the traditional Chinese calendar. Snow had already settled on the grasslands and surrounding mountains. As dusk fell over the plateau, the wind picked up. Inside his new home, Sonam Dondrup fed a few more pieces of dried yak dung into the stove, and the tea in the kettle soon bubbled again. Outside, meanwhile, smoke rose from chimneys in the fading light. ■

item.title: China launches Shenzhou-24 spaceship, opening Tiangong space station to first foreign astronaut
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
* China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft, sending three astronauts, including a Pakistani astronaut, into the orbiting Tiangong space station. * The Shenzhou-24 mission, carried out by Chinese mission commander and spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marks the first joint flight consisting of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. Ali also became the first foreign astronaut to board Tiangong. * China's manned space program has consistently adhered to the principle of peaceful utilization, equality and mutual benefit, and common development, while actively promoting international exchanges and cooperation and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind in outer space. by Xinhua writers Li Minghao, Yi Ling and Quan Xiaoshu JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft on Wednesday, sending three astronauts, including a Pakistani astronaut, into the orbiting Tiangong space station. The Shenzhou-24 mission, carried out by Chinese mission commander and spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marks the first joint flight consisting of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. Ali also became the first foreign astronaut to board Tiangong. Zhang Jingbo, spokesperson for the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), described the joint flight as a landmark achievement in bilateral cooperation as the two countries mark the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations this year, and an important manifestation of their traditional friendship. China's manned space program has consistently adhered to the principle of peaceful utilization, equality and mutual benefit, and common development, while actively promoting international exchanges and cooperation and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind in outer space, Zhang said at a news conference on Tuesday. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the United Nations welcomed the peaceful use of outer space and the international cooperation this mission represents. Aboard a Long March-2F carrier rocket, the spaceship blasted off at 8:18 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China. About 10 minutes after liftoff, the spaceship separated from the rocket and entered its designated orbit. The CMSA declared the launch "a complete success." The spacecraft completed a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tianhe, the station's core module, in about 3.5 hours. The Shenzhou-23 crew aboard Tiangong opened the hatch at 2:35 p.m. and welcomed the new arrivals. The two crews then took group pictures marking the ninth space get-together in China's aerospace history. After completing a short-term joint flight, Ali will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft alongside two Shenzhou-23 crew members. The other two Shenzhou-24 astronauts will stay in orbit for roughly six months along with Shenzhou-23 astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, who has already spent six months in orbit and will remain aboard Tiangong to complete a year-long stay experiment. JOINT EXPERIMENTS More than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests are planned for the Shenzhou-24 mission, covering space life sciences, space material science, microgravity fluid physics and combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine and new space technologies, according to the CMSA. Four China-Pakistan cooperative projects in the fields of biotechnology and materials will be conducted during the Shenzhou-24 mission, and Ali will conduct an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria, which was proposed by the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO). The experiment is expected to provide a biological basis and data support for oxygen regeneration and biomanufacturing at future space stations and deep-space bases, said Chen Mengyun, who is in charge of international cooperation projects at the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization under the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Another cooperative project, led by the University of Agriculture, Faisalabad in Pakistan, will expose 32 quinoa seed samples to the space environment outside the station for about one year to investigate their stress tolerance and longevity, with the aim of screening for superior varieties. Describing Pakistan as one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change, Pakistani Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal said that the country needs smart and climate-resilient agriculture. "The mission gives Pakistani scientists rare access to space laboratories, offering potential breakthroughs to boost productivity and climate resilience," he told Xinhua. The other two experiments will focus on multilayer graphene-based hybrid composites and solar-heated self-healing carbon fiber composites, Chen said. Pakistani Ambassador to China Syed Ali Asad Gillani said the four experiments in orbit will not only benefit Pakistani researchers, but also help advance the prosperity and development of all humanity. China-Pakistan space cooperation spans more than three decades. In 1990, Pakistan's first experimental satellite, Badr-1, was launched aboard a Chinese rocket from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center. More recently, China launched Pakistan's cube satellite aboard the Chang'e-6 probe in 2024 and placed a Pakistani remote-sensing satellite in orbit via a Long March-6 rocket in April 2026. COOPERATIVE TEAM To support the joint flight, the Chinese side prepared bilingual Chinese-English manuals, provided food tailored to Ali's cultural and dietary habits, and tailored training and ceremonial attire for the Pakistani. According to Shi Yusheng, an expert with the Astronaut Center of China, the center devised multiple methods to help Ali master Chinese commands and terminology critical for spaceflight. Beyond basic language courses, Ali received intensive training in high-frequency spaceflight vocabulary and commands. Later in the program, he was also taught classical Chinese poetry. "With tight timelines and heavy tasks, we focused on spacecraft operations, pressure emergency response, fault handling and scientific experiments, and conducted high-frequency joint training to ensure the mission's success," Tang, the Shenzhou-24 mission commander, said at Tuesday's media briefing. Wu, the mission flight engineer, said Ali had worked diligently to learn Chinese, while the Chinese crew used English as a supplementary communication tool. Through sustained effort, the crew progressed from merely understanding each other to anticipating each other's actions. Ali can now communicate with his Chinese counterparts in Chinese. He described mastering flight skills, learning Chinese and forging close bonds with his Chinese crewmates as key gains from his training. Ali said China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time. "Now it is time to show this great achievement in orbit and send the world a message that we work hand in hand for the peaceful utilization of space," he said. In an interview with Xinhua, the Pakistani ambassador to China described the joint flight as taking bilateral relations "from Earth to space," calling it a dream come true for more than 250 million Pakistanis and "an excellent model for South-South cooperation." MULTIPLE TASKS The Shenzhou-24 mission's main objectives are to complete an in-orbit crew rotation with the Shenzhou-23 crew, maintain routine station operations, conduct space science and application work, and carry out maintenance, public outreach and payload tests. One of the highlights is China's first year-long in-orbit stay experiment. The year-long test will establish a new system for studying the human body in space, conduct interdisciplinary frontier scientific experiments, explore and answer intrinsic mechanisms of human adaptation and remodeling in a spaceflight environment, build a space-human-body research database combining macro and micro perspectives, and produce a batch of original outcomes, said Zhang, the CMSA spokesperson. In addition, the test will further accumulate practical experience in astronaut support technologies, enrich and improve the major safeguarding systems for in-orbit health, work and daily life, and steadily enhance the astronaut residency support capabilities of China's space station, he added. (Video reporters: Li Guoli, Liu Yi, Da Rihan, Zhang Sheng, Fang Kuan, Wei Ying, Hong Liang, Sha Shiyuan and Yang Zhigang; Video editors:Li Ziwei, Zhu Cong, Long Lingyu, Zheng Qingbin and Li Qin) ■

item.title: Shenzhou-24 astronauts, including first foreigner, enter China's Tiangong space station

FOCUS | Shenzhou-24 astronauts, including first foreigner, enter China's Tiangong space station-Xinhua FOCUS | Shenzhou-24 astronauts, including first foreigner, enter China's Tiangong space station Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-11-25 18:01:30 JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Shenzhou-24 crew, comprising Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, entered China's Tiangong space station on Wednesday. Serving as a payload specialist, Ali has made history by becoming the first foreigner to board Tiangong. The astronaut trio took off at 8:18 a.m. (Beijing Time) the same day aboard China's Shenzhou-24 spaceship from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China. The Shenzhou-23 crew in orbit opened the hatch of the space station at 2:35 p.m. and welcomed the new arrivals, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). After entering the space station, the Shenzhou-24 crew met with the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who have been in orbit for about six months. The two crews then took group pictures of the ninth space get-together in China's aerospace history. They will now start a new in-orbit handover round.

item.title: Xi says joint space exploration by Chinese, Pakistani astronauts vivid embodiment of deep-rooted friendship
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
BEIJING, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that the joint space exploration by astronauts from China and Pakistan is a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries. It marks another important achievement in bilateral cooperation, Xi said while exchanging congratulations with Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on the joint spaceflight mission. In the message, Xi said that he was glad to learn of a Pakistani astronaut's successful entry into space aboard a Chinese Shenzhou spaceship for the first time, making him the first foreign astronaut to inhabit China's space station. Xi extended his warm congratulations to the Pakistani government and people, as well as to astronauts and space professionals from both countries on behalf of the Chinese government and people. Xi noted that China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners, saying that the friendship between the two countries has remained rock-solid and unbreakable since diplomatic ties were established 75 years ago. Emphasizing that China's space station is an ark of peace, friendship and cooperation, Xi said that China stands ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to advance the peaceful use of outer space, deepen international space cooperation, and improve global governance in outer space, to ensure that outer space exploration delivers greater benefits to the humanity. For his part, Zardari expressed profound appreciation to the Chinese government and the brotherly Chinese people on behalf of the Pakistani government and people. He said the historic space cooperation between Pakistan and China and the first Pakistani astronaut entering China's space station come as the two countries commemorate the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations. Such cooperation demonstrates China's remarkable progress in space science and technology, its firm commitment to the peaceful use of outer space, and the significance of building a community with a shared future for humanity, Zardari said, adding that it will further strengthen bilateral friendship, and promote the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between the two countries to a higher level. ■

item.title: Xi urges advancing building of Party regulations, institutions
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
BEIJING, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged continuous and high-quality advancement in the building of regulations and institutions of the Communist Party of China (CPC), and upholding rule-based governance as the basic approach to governing the Party. Xi, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction on the work related to Party regulations and institutions. Xi said the CPC has made solid efforts and achieved notable achievements in strengthening Party regulations and institutions over the past five years. To provide institutional guarantees for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance and ensuring the Party remains the strong leadership core in building socialism with Chinese characteristics, Xi urged enhanced efforts in the systematic integration, education and enforcement of Party institutions, as well as in improving the alignment and coordination of Party rules and regulations with state laws and regulations. Xi's instruction was conveyed at a national meeting on the work related to Party regulations held in Beijing on Tuesday and Wednesday. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and a member of the Secretariat of the CPC Central Committee, attends and addresses a national meeting on the work related to Party regulations in Beijing, capital of China. An important instruction by Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed at the meeting held in Beijing on Tuesday and Wednesday. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei) Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and a member of the Secretariat of the CPC Central Committee, attended and addressed the meeting. Running the Party through institutions and regulations is one of the core meanings of Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building, Cai noted, calling for efforts to enhance the level of running the Party through regulations across the board. ■
